context_blurb:
Every year the world turns from warm to cold and back: summer evenings stay light past bedtime, winter afternoons go dark before supper, and snow, blossom and falling leaves come round in turn. The seasons rule what farmers plant and what you wear, and their cause is a lean you can see on any classroom globe.

Earth spins on its axis, an imaginary line through the North and South Poles, and that axis leans. Stand a pencil straight up on the flat plane in which Earth circles the Sun, and Earth's axis tips about 23.5 degrees away from that pencil. Measured from the plane itself, the axis stands at about 66.5 degrees, so the two numbers add up to 90.

What makes the lean matter is that the axis keeps pointing the same way all year, wherever Earth is on its trip. Polaris, the North Star, shows it: the axis's northern end aims almost straight at that star, and the star hangs in the same spot in the northern sky all year. On one side of the trip, the Northern Hemisphere, the half of Earth north of the equator, leans toward the Sun; six months later, on the far side, it leans away. The seasons come from the tilt of Earth's axis, which turns each half of the planet toward the Sun and then away from it, once a year. Carry a tilted ball round a lamp, its tilt always aimed at the same wall, and first its top half, then its bottom half, leans toward the light.

So the two halves of Earth always have opposite seasons. In late December, while snow settles over Canada and the north has winter, the Southern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun and its summer is beginning. In Australia, Christmas comes in early summer, a day for barbecues and the beach.

Many people believe summer comes when Earth swings closer to the Sun. That is wrong. The gap between Earth and the Sun changes by only about 5 million kilometres out of some 150 million. Earth passes closest to the Sun in early January, at about 147 million kilometres, and is farthest in early July, at about 152 million. The north has its winter while Earth is nearest the Sun.

The leaning half warms for two reasons. First, its noon Sun climbs high. A low winter Sun sends its light in at a slant, and a slanting beam spreads the same sunlight over a wider patch of ground, so each patch gets less warmth. Shine a flashlight straight down on paper, then tip it: the spot of light grows bigger and dimmer. Second, its days are long and its nights short, so the Sun has more hours to warm it.

At the equator, day stays close to 12 hours all year round. In late June, with the North Pole tipped toward the Sun, more of each spin keeps the far north in sunlight, so the days grow longer the farther north you travel. North of the Arctic Circle the Sun does not set at all, giving 24 hours of daylight: the midnight sun.

Around June 21 comes the June solstice, when the north leans most toward the Sun and has the most daylight of the year, its longest day, while the Southern Hemisphere has its shortest. The main line of Stonehenge, in England, points at that day's sunrise.

Midway between the solstices come the equinoxes, around March 20, when spring begins in the north, and around September 22, when autumn does. Earth's axis is still tilted then, but it leans neither toward the Sun nor away from it. Day and night are then about equal almost everywhere on Earth, close to 12 hours each; only at the North and South Poles does the Sun stay up for a few days, skimming along the horizon. Equinox comes from Latin words for equal night.

Yet the hottest weeks come later than the longest day. Far north of the equator, a thermometer read every afternoon for a year shows the warmest weeks in July and August, a month or two after the noon Sun stood highest. The oceans cover most of Earth and are slow to warm up, so the air over land and sea goes on warming for weeks after the solstice. This delay is called the lag of the seasons.
